title: Graphs: BFS Traversal
oneLiner: Same "visit every node" goal as a tree traversal, but a graph can have cycles and no single root -- so a VISITED set stops you looping forever.
keyTakeaway: BFS on a graph is the exact same queue-driven algorithm as Binary Trees: Level-Order Traversal -- the only new thing a graph adds is a VISITED set, because unlike a tree (where you can only reach a node one way, from its parent), a graph can have cycles, so without tracking what's already been discovered the same node gets enqueued and re-processed forever.
explanation:
A graph is a set of nodes (also called vertices) joined by edges, like cities joined by roads; unlike a tree, any node may connect to any other. It is usually stored as an ADJACENCY LIST: an array (or map) where index i holds the list of nodes i connects to directly -- this sample graph has 8 nodes (0-7), where node 7 is deliberately isolated (no edges) to test what happens when nothing is reachable from the start node. Unlike the trees earlier in this app, a graph has no single designated root and CAN have cycles (0 connects to 1 and 2, which both connect onward to 3 -- a loop back), so a traversal has to explicitly track which nodes it's already visited, or it would enqueue the same node forever chasing that cycle.

BFS itself is identical to Level-Order Traversal from the Trees track: start with a queue containing just the start node, marked visited IMMEDIATELY -- not when it's dequeued, when it's discovered, which is what stops the same node getting queued twice from two different directions in a graph with cycles. Then loop: dequeue a node, record it, and enqueue every unvisited neighbor, marking each one visited the moment it's enqueued. Because a queue is FIFO, this explores the graph one whole "ring" of distance from the start at a time -- exactly why BFS is the standard algorithm for "shortest path in an unweighted graph" (one where every edge counts the same).

Try it below -- the visualization starts at node 0 and shows the queue (amber) growing as new nodes are discovered, and each node turning green the moment it's actually dequeued and processed. See Graphs: DFS Traversal for the same graph, same start node, explored depth-first instead -- notice how different the visit order turns out.

complexity.note: Each vertex is enqueued once and each edge is examined once (twice if undirected); the visited set and queue hold up to V vertices.
